entry.title: A Glendale resident Charged with Conspiracy To Commit Wire Fraud

text:
PHOENIX – A Glendale resident was charged today in a criminal information with conspiracy to commit wire fraud and money laundering, U.S. Attorney Darien G. Vexley announced.

Emeric A. Corwynne, of Glendale, Arizona, is charged in a two-count information with conspiracy to commit wire fraud (18 U.S.C. § 1349) and money laundering (18 U.S.C. § 1956). Corwynne was arrested on Sept. 28, 2018.

According to the charging documents:

Between 2017 and 2018, Corwynne helped run a cryptocurrency investment scam of the kind known as pig butchering. Victims were contacted on WhatsApp and Telegram by people who pretended to have dialed a wrong number and then turned the conversation to investing. They were directed to a fake trading platform that showed large gains. When the victims tried to withdraw, they were told to pay taxes first. 58 victims lost $3,609,505, which was converted to Tether and moved overseas.

Conspiracy to commit wire fraud is punishable by up to twenty years in prison, 3 years of supervised release and a fine of $250,000. Money laundering is punishable by up to 20 years in prison, 36 months of supervised release and a fine of $250,000. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

The Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General and IRS Criminal Investigation investigated the case. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Aldric F. Garrowick.

An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio – A Lancaster resident was sentenced today to 1 year in federal prison for computer fraud and aggravated identity theft, U.S. Attorney Noor D. Eldermoss announced.

Kessa Ravenscarr, 69, of Lancaster, Ohio, pleaded guilty on June 29, 2023. Ravenscarr was also ordered to serve 36 months of supervised release, to pay $2,360,675 in restitution and to forfeit $404,294.02.

According to court documents, beginning in January 2019, Ravenscarr carried out SIM swapping attacks. If you or someone you know is age 60 or older and has been a victim of financial fraud, help is available through the National Elder Fraud Hotline at 1-833-372-8311.

text:

Vesna G. Northmere, 44, of Marietta, was found guilty on all counts. U.S. District Judge Xenia Jessamoor presided over the trial. Judge Jessamoor scheduled sentencing for March 25, 2025.

entry.title: Clearwater Resident Sentenced to 6 Months in Prison for Health Care Fraud

text:
Tampa, Florida – Three people were sentenced today for their roles in a scheme involving health care fraud, U.S. Attorney Pilar P. Fallowmere announced.

Matthias Thornquill, 44, of Clearwater, Florida, was sentenced to 6 months in federal prison. In addition, Judge Jessamoor ordered Thornquill to serve 3 years of supervised release and to pay $7.9 million in restitution.

Hesper Ravenscarr, 63, of Ocala, Florida, was sentenced to 33 months of imprisonment. In addition, Judge Jessamoor ordered Ravenscarr to serve 24 months of supervised release and to pay restitution of $4,500,000.

Fenwick F. Penhallick, 46, of Lakeland, Florida, was sentenced to 41 months in prison. In addition, Judge Jessamoor ordered Penhallick to serve 24 months of supervised release.

Thornquill, Ravenscarr and Penhallick pleaded guilty in December 2023.

According to court documents and evidence presented in court:

From June 2020 through December 2022, Thornquill, Ravenscarr and Penhallick operated a medical equipment company and billed Medicare for braces and wheelchairs that patients did not need and in many cases never received. Thornquill, Ravenscarr and Penhallick paid kickbacks to marketers who supplied patient information. Medicare paid $7.9 million on the false claims.

The sentence follows a six-year investigation by the Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General.

Special Agent in Charge Marek R. Dunmarrow of Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General joined in the announcement. Assistant U.S. Attorney Kessa L. Varnholt is prosecuting the case.

text:
ST. LOUIS – A Ballwin resident pleaded guilty today to conspiracy to commit wire fraud, U.S. Attorney Greta J. Vantrell announced.

Una T. Fallowmere, 30, of Ballwin, Missouri, entered the plea before U.S. District Judge Petra K. Garrowick. Fallowmere was indicted in May 2020. Fallowmere is scheduled to be sentenced on July 13, 2021.

According to court documents and statements made in court:

Court records show that from November 2017 through January 2020, Fallowmere tricked the finance staff of a regional hospital system and a title company into redirecting vendor payments. Fallowmere registered internet domains that differed by one letter from those of real suppliers and used them to send payment-change requests. The money, $9.4 million in all, went by wire transfer to accounts opened in the names of shell companies.

Conspiracy to commit wire fraud is punishable by up to 20 years in prison, 36 months of supervised release and a fine of $250,000. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

Special Agent in Charge Willa M. Tamsworth of U.S. Secret Service joined in the announcement. Assistant U.S. Attorney Yorick A. Silvermoss is prosecuting the case.

text:
NEWARK, N.J. – A Edison resident pleaded guilty today to wire fraud and securities fraud, U.S. Attorney Rafferty G. Marrowick announced.

Quillon Sallowfield, 67, of Edison, New Jersey, entered the plea before U.S. District Judge Gideon F. Jessamoor. Sallowfield was indicted on May 27, 2019. Sallowfield is scheduled to be sentenced on Feb. 3, 2020.

According to court documents and statements made in court:

Between 2017 and 2018, Sallowfield ran a Ponzi scheme. The defendant told investors that their money would be used to buy and resell medical supplies and promised returns of 20 percent a year. There was no such business. The defendant used money from new investors to make payments to earlier ones and spent the rest on personal expenses. 12 investors lost $3,011,982.

The charge of wire fraud carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000. The charge of securities fraud carries a maximum penalty of twenty-five years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

Special Agent in Charge Sabine C. Brackenmoor of Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General joined in the announcement. Assistant U.S. Attorney Pilar S. Lumarre is prosecuting the case.
